summary:
Astronaut Health Monitoring Software by the Phoenix Astronomy Team, NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

This prototype supports astronauts on long missions with limited contact with Earth. A wearable streams body signals, and the astronaut adds manual measurements, such as blood pressure, temperature and body mass, in a Daily Check Up. The software compares each reading with the astronaut's own baseline for the active mode (Regular, Sleep or Exercise). It detects abnormal values and symptoms, then shows one short, plain instruction at a time. It never diagnoses; it only names actions and what the problem is about.

Alerts have three levels: Watch, Act and Emergency. The software covers eighteen emergencies and twelve condition patterns. An SOS button, a strong tap or a voice command calls the crew at once, and Crew Aid lets a helper describe the astronaut's symptoms. Mental health entries stay private. Everything is saved permanently with its time. Because there is no real hardware, a Simulation page supplies every value.

That is about 165 words.

Astronaut Health Monitoring Software: Project Description

Phoenix Astronomy Team · NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · Prototype

1. What the software is, and the principles it never breaks

Purpose. A web app (it runs in a browser, no installation) for astronauts on long missions with limited contact with Earth. A wearable streams body signals continuously and the astronaut makes some manual measurements. The software detects abnormal readings and symptoms, tells the astronaut what to do in simple steps, alerts crew and medical support, and keeps monitoring until the problem is over or handed to medical care. The software never diagnoses. It detects patterns, decides how urgent they are, and shows safe actions.

Where it runs. The same web app opens in a browser on the astronaut's wrist screen and on the station's screens (laptops, tablets). The layout adapts to the screen size. The wrist screen is the main one, because the SOS (button, strong tap) and alarms must be on the astronaut at all times.

This is a prototype for testing. There is no real hardware. The Simulation page, opened from the dashboard, supplies every value. The software must behave exactly as it would with real data.

Core rules.

  1. Check emergencies first. Only when none matches, check the milder condition patterns.
  2. Every comparison depends on the active mode: Sleep, Regular or Exercise.
  3. Missing or bad data is never treated as normal.
  4. Danger limits and dangerous symptoms act at once in every mode and never wait for a repeat reading.
  5. The astronaut sees one short instruction at a time, in plain words. No instruction needs gravity: never "lie down", "sit", "stand", "turn up" or "turn down". Use "secure yourself" (hold a handrail or strap in) and "stay still".
  6. Instructions never name a diagnosis. They name actions.
  7. Medicines, oxygen, advanced procedures and tourniquets are shown only as "Use the item your mission plan names."
  8. Everything measured or entered is saved permanently with its time. Nothing is ever erased or overwritten.

Alert levels. Level 0: normal. Level 1 (Watch): one unusual reading, no danger symptom, recheck. Level 2 (Act): a confirmed or persistent concern, instructions shown, medical notified. Level 3 (Emergency): danger, crew alerted at once.

Design decisions.

  1. The software announces emergencies by itself. Every emergency screen has a "No emergency" button for false alarms. For an emergency that no device detects and that the astronaut cannot describe, there is the SOS (an on screen button that simulates a physical button, a strong tap on the screen, or a voice command. While help is coming, the software keeps searching for the cause. A crew mate who comes to help can then describe the astronaut's symptoms with Crew Aid.
  2. No medical screen. Messages to medical are simulated: the software records "sent to medical (simulated)" and shows it in Records.
  3. Five event states only: Watch, Act, Emergency, Monitoring, Closed.
  4. Voice read out and spoken "Done" are simulated (tap or type works). Every step screen has a Read aloud button.
  5. "This is about". Alert and emergency screens never name a condition, but they say what the problem is about (heart rate, breathing, temperature…).

2. Screens and flow

Look of every screen: dark space background (deep blue nebula and stars), glass panels, cyan and teal accents, large touch targets (at least 44 px). Red is used only for SOS and emergencies, orange for alerts.

2.1 Login

Fields: Serial number (this is the astronaut ID) and First/Last name. Button: LOG IN. Exit only.

  • Known serial number: load the stored profile, baselines and full history. Nothing is asked again.

2.2 Dashboard (home page)

  • Top bar: Return · active mode banner (Regular, Sleep Mode or Exercise Mode) · astronaut ID, mission day and time · Log out · Exit. If an event is active, a second banner shows its state. Logging out erases nothing.
    1. Daily Check Up (wide, first): everything the astronaut measures on their own, with a count of what is due.
    2. Sleep: opens the Sleep screen and turns Sleep Mode on.
    3. Exercise: opens the Exercise screen and turns Exercise Mode on.
    4. Crew Aid: used by a crew mate who comes to help another astronaut.
    5. Records: Now, History, Past 7 days, Events, Private.
    6. Reminders, with a count.
    7. Simulation: the test page.

Only one mode can be on at a time. Turning on one mode closes the other first.

SOS. A large red button on the dashboard and a small one in the top bar of every other screen, in every mode. It is a simulation of the physical SOS button a real wrist device would have. Pressing it, tapping the screen strongly, or saying the voice command calls the crew at once, and the cause search starts.

2.3 Simulation page

The test page, opened from the dashboard tile. It reads the current mode first (set on the dashboard) and shows it at the top; every case and every run uses that mode.

Left section: body and devices.

  1. A picture of the human body (front view) with each device drawn at its place, numbered:
    • Worn, measuring all the time: 1 Chest patch (chest: heart rate, ECG, ECG pause, HRV, breathing rate, no breathing time, signal quality), 2 Wrist device (wrist: SpO2, skin temperature, activity, sleep hours; it also carries the SOS button), 3 Dosimeter (chest pocket: radiation dose rate, mission dose, solar particle warning).
    • Used by hand on the body: 5 Arm cuff (upper arm), 6 Thermometer (mouth or ear), 7 Fingertip oximeter (finger), 8 SLAMMD (holds the whole body), 9 Near vision card (in front of the eyes).
  2. Under the picture, the devices not attached to the body are named: 4 Cabin sensors (module wall: oxygen, pressure, CO2, contaminants, smoke), 10 Urine kit and drink containers, 11 App form (mood, stress), 12 12 lead ECG unit (a crew mate helps), 13 Ultrasound (only when medical directs).
  3. Three case buttons: Normal, Alert, Emergency. For the chosen case and the current mode, every device lists all of its variables with a suggested value (all 33 variables). The values that create the alert or emergency are coloured, and one line says what was changed.
  4. USE fills every suggested value into the right section.

Right section: everything that is measured. One input per variable, in three groups: continuous worn on the body, continuous cabin sensors, manual. Then "Hold these values for … minutes" and RUN. The result shows under RUN: "all normal" (nothing happens), "Alert (Level 2)" or "EMERGENCY", with what it is about and a link to the screen that opened.

More test controls (folded under the right section): A profile and preflight baseline (prefilled with the demo profile), D history counters, E controls (crew responds, crew arrived, astronaut responsive, per signal state, strong tap, voice command, erase), F clock buttons, G thresholds.

2.4 Mode screens

  • Sleep screen: dim night background, moon icon, time, "Sleep mode on · monitoring quietly · reminders silent". Buttons: Crew Aid (always shown, so the astronaut can help a crew mate without turning Sleep Mode off first), I'm awake · end sleep mode, small SOS, Return, Exit.
  • Exercise screen: title EXERCISE MODE, type, intensity and time, Live vitals (large heart rate with ECG trace, heart rate zone bar against the zone ceiling), SpO2, breathing, skin temperature, activity, an Alerts this session list (every Level 1 prompt and Level 2 alert of the session, newest first), End exercise, small SOS, Return, Exit.

2.5 Alert and emergency screens

  • Alert (Level 2): "We noticed something", "This is about: [category]", the pattern's steps with Done, what was found, the reminders that were added, and "Medical has been notified (simulated)".
  • Emergency: Title EMERGENCY, "This is about: [category]", the top note, one large step at a time with DONE and READ ALOUD, the list of all steps, live vitals, crew status, "Are you OK?", "The crew has not arrived", "No emergency".

4. What happens in an emergency

4.1 When any emergency opens

When any emergency opens (Level 3), do these steps in this order. Steps 2 to 4 happen at the same moment.

  1. Declare. Set Emergency state. End Sleep Mode or Exercise Mode. Store "mode at onset". Sound the alarm (loudest, with lights, in Sleep). In Exercise, the first instruction is "Stop. Let the equipment stop safely." Show the top note: "Other crew are informed. Waiting for a response." (nothing is really sent). Show the "No emergency" button on every emergency screen.
    • Crew responds within 30 seconds: show Display B (the astronaut is stabilised until crew arrive).
    • No response by 30 seconds: Display A turns on by itself (the astronaut handles the emergency alone, as safely as possible). Queue a note to ground and medical. Nothing repeats.
    • A response after 30 seconds: switch to Display B.
    • While the timer runs (the first 30 seconds), show step 1 of Display A. Step 1 is the same action in A and B for every emergency, so nothing is lost when the display switches.
  2. Show steps one at a time, in large text, read aloud. The astronaut taps Done or says "Done" to see the next step. Steps shared by A and B have the same step ID and keep their Done mark when the display switches. Steps never advance on their own. After the last step show the Stay safe screen: "Stay secured. Stay still. Breathe slowly. Help is coming." (or "Help is being called." if nobody answered), with a "Show steps again" button.
  3. "The crew has not arrived" (button or voice) on Display B: make one new call to all crew (simulated), restart the 30 second timer, show "Crew called again." No answer in 30 seconds: Display A turns on. This works once per emergency. A second press shows "Crew was already called again. Stay secured." and is only recorded. The simulator's "Crew arrived" button ends the waiting and shows "Crew is with you."
  4. Keep measuring. Pattern steps for non emergencies are paused while an emergency is open. Measurements and symptoms keep updating the record.
  5. "No emergency" button. Ask "Are you sure?" On yes: close the emergency part as "closed by astronaut". Keep reading the signals. If a measured danger value is still present on the next reading, open the emergency again at once. A symptom only trigger reopens only if the symptom is reported again. Follow up reminders for that kind of event are not cancelled.
  6. Never close silently. The software never closes an emergency without the astronaut's confirmation.

4.2 SOS (an emergency that nothing detects and the astronaut cannot describe)

Purpose. Some emergencies are not detected by any device, and the astronaut may be unable to describe them (for example E14 or E15 symptoms, or anything not in the lists). The SOS lets the astronaut call for help with a single action, without describing anything.

The SOS button is a simulation of a physical button. A real mission would use a hardware button on the wrist device. We cannot build hardware, so the prototype shows the button on the dashboard instead. It is large, red, always visible on every screen and in every mode, and it behaves exactly like the physical button would.

Three ways to call, all in every mode:

  1. Press the SOS button on the dashboard (stands for the physical button).
  2. Tap the screen strongly (a hard tap or knock on the wrist device). In the prototype, the Simulation page's "Strong tap" button stands for it.
  3. Say the voice command "SOS", "Call crew" or "Emergency" (phrases editable). In the prototype, typing the phrase in the Simulation page's "Voice command" field stands for saying it.

5. Event states

State

Meaning

Watch

Level 1. One recheck pending

Act

Level 2. Instructions shown, rechecks scheduled, medical notified

Emergency

Level 3

Monitoring

After an emergency is closed, or when a Level 2 event's criteria are met but a caution period or sign off remains, or for Ongoing patterns

Closed

Over. Stays in the history

6. Crew Aid (a helper describes another astronaut's symptoms)

When it is used. A crew mate comes to help an astronaut who cannot describe what is wrong: after an SOS, after any crew alert, or when they find the astronaut unwell. The helper opens Crew Aid on their own device (from the dashboard, or from the Sleep screen without ending Sleep Mode). It must be quick.

The screen.

  • Top banner: who needs help and why ("SOS from [astronaut ID] · cause not known · module · time") and what the cause search has found so far. The patient is taken from the latest SOS or crew alert; if there is none, the helper picks them from the crew list. The helper's own ID is stored as the reporter.
  • Describe symptoms: a large text box where the helper types (or dictates) what they see, and an ANALYZE button next to it.
  • Questions: a box that shows quick questions only if the app did not understand the symptoms.
  • Instructions: a box where the steps appear as soon as the analysis or the answers are done.

7. Mental health (private)

  1. Options: low mood, worry or fear, stress, trouble sleeping, loneliness, irritability, trouble concentrating, low motivation, conflict with crew. Ask mood 0 to 10 and stress 0 to 10.
  2. Always ask: "Are you having thoughts of harming yourself or anyone else, or do you feel you cannot stay safe?" Yes: open E16 at once, privately. No score is needed.
  3. Mental health entries are stored with a Private tag.

8. Daily Check Up (manual measurements)

Everything the astronaut measures on their own. The screen has one row (a rectangle) per measurement, as many rows as there are manual measurements, each with three parts:

  • Left, what to measure: the name, the device, when to do it, and a status chip ("Due now", "Done 07:05", "Weekly · due", "When asked").
  • Middle, How: a button that opens the steps below the row. Tapping it again hides them.
  • Right, Input: the fields for the result, and Save.

Save stores the value with its time. A field left empty is recorded as "not measured" and is left out of every comparison. In a test, the Simulation page can supply the same values. A Report a symptom button sits at the top of the screen.

Measurement

Device

Blood pressure

Automated upper arm cuff

Core temperature

Mission thermometer, the same type every time

Fingertip SpO2

Fingertip pulse oximeter

Body mass

SLAMMD (Space Linear Acceleration Mass Measurement Device). A normal scale does not work in microgravity. SLAMMD has two springs that push the astronaut with a known force (F) along a short track, and measures the acceleration (a). The device computes mass = F ÷ a. Accuracy about 0.2 kg

Visual acuity

Near vision card

Urine check

Mission urine test kit

Fluid log

Mission drink containers

Mood and stress (private)

This app

12 lead ECG

Mission 12 lead ECG unit

Ultrasound

Mission ultrasound

9. Reminders

Order on screen. Condition reminders first (from events, newest event first), then Daily reminders, then Mine. Inside each group, by time.

Daily reminders (default list).

  • "Drink water" every 2 hours while awake, with the amount from the fluid plan divided by 8.
  • "Exercise today: [type] for [minutes]" using the rotation Aerobic 30, Resistance 30, High intensity interval 25.
  • "Daily Check Up" in the morning after 5 minutes of rest.
  • Weekly: "Body mass (SLAMMD)" on the same day each week, in the morning before eating and after the toilet, and "Eye test".
  • "Get ready for sleep" 60 minutes before the usual bedtime.
  • Mental health: "Two minutes of slow breathing" daily, "How is your mood today?" every evening, "Call family or a friend" weekly.

Condition reminders. Created from the event (examples: "Measure your heart rate and blood pressure" every 4 hours for 24 hours; "Take your temperature" every 4 hours; "Do the eye test" next morning; "How do you feel now?"). The astronaut can mark each one Done, which clears only that occurrence. They cannot be deleted and keep coming until the event closes. Snooze: up to 2 times, 10 minutes each. Closing by "No emergency" does not cancel them.

10. Records

  • Now: live values from the simulator with units, mode, signal quality and last update. Missing values show "No data".
  • History: everything stored in the database for this identity, newest first, each line with its date and time. Filters: measurements, manual inputs, symptoms (own or by crew mate), modes, events, alerts and calls, reminders. Private entries are not shown here.
  • Past 7 days: read from the database. Continuous signals as hourly averages, manual signals as single entries, each with its time. If fewer than 7 days are stored, show the days that exist. Days with no data show "No data", never invented values.
  • Events: records of events created during runs, labelled "Simulated run", with handover summaries and responder checklists.
  • Private tab for mental health entries.

Mental health data and private consultations are marked Private and appear only in the Private tab. Records are kept permanently in the database. Logging out does not erase them.
